claims.text: The target alloy is a homogeneous, coarse-grained, quaternary equiatomic FCC solid solution.
A moderate stacking-fault energy suppresses deformation twinning and phase transformation at room temperature while permitting dislocation accumulation.
Elevated-temperature yielding or deformation is dislocation based.
Yield strength becomes insensitive to strain rate between 673 and 873 K over strain rates of 10^-4 to 10^-1 s^-1.
The strain-rate-insensitive plateau is caused by a transition from dislocation glide to an edge-dislocation super-jogging mechanism.
A suitable stacking-fault-energy window can prevent early phase transformation and amorphization while retaining the proposed super-jog mechanism.
At intermediate temperatures, climb or cross-slip of edge dislocations produces thermal super-jogs.
Thermal super-jogs pin dislocation lines and act as strong barriers to slip.
Super-jog formation creates competition between work hardening by dislocation accumulation and dynamic recovery by jog annihilation.
Jog-formation activation energy, rather than strain rate, dominates the flow stress in the plateau regime.
Ductility decreases slightly in the intermediate-temperature regime because dislocations accumulate at super-jog barriers.
Deformation in the proposed plateau regime produces no deformation twins, HCP martensite, or amorphous bands.
If stacking-fault energy is too low, TWIP or TRIP dominates and causes strain-rate sensitivity.
If stacking-fault energy is too high, super-jogging may cease to be rate limiting.
Standard FCC alloys typically show a monotonic positive strain-rate sensitivity caused by dislocation drag or thermally activated kink-pair formation.
The temperature range of the plateau depends on the alloy-specific activation energy for jog formation.
Nanoscale precipitates reported in PMC10453588 could provide additional pinning and mimic a strength plateau.
Phase transformation and amorphization can be distinguished from dislocation glide through phase-fraction measurements and characteristic TEM or diffraction signatures.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis says stacking-fault energy should be sufficiently low to prevent early phase transformation, whereas the boundary states that low stacking-fault energy promotes TWIP/TRIP. A possible intermediate window is implied, but the direction of the stated SFE effect is internally inconsistent.
